Well, the issue with zero downvoting, is that you might end up with a YouTube style comment system.

Once the discussion becomes large enough, a very small group of people, say less then 1% of userbase, will consistently upvote comments in support of extreme views such as Nazism and racism. Since there is no way for the 99% of viewers who do not support these views to check them, it can leave casual viewers with the impression that a larger proportion of site users support these extreme views than they actually do, and it produces an unnecessary source of fuel for those engaged in reactionary politics.

That said, I also think there are also obvious problems with systems of a widespread downvoting, as it enables a 51-98% majority to completely suppress discussion by a 49-2% minority.

I think the current inclination of voat to allow downvoting, but to limit or restrict it in some fashion, may be a pragmatic compromise.

Well perhaps that leaves us with a Web of Trust as a long term solution.

Imagine each user has a list of other users associated with their account, which they either mark as trusted or untrusted.

When you trust a user, you are also implicitly trusting the users the trust to some degree, and distrusting the users they distrust to some degree.

When you view comments on a page, it is not sorted by karma, and you do not view upvotes or downvotes next to each commenter. Instead, it is perhaps sorted by trust, and you view a trust score and a distrust score next to each comment.

You could compute a trust score for a users comment by examining whether you have trusted them directly (1st degree), by examining whether anyone you trusted trusts them (2nd degree), and examining whether anyone you trust trusts someone who trusts them (3rd degree), and weighting this appropriately.

If you suspected an account was compromised by a spammer or corporate advertiser, you would be allowed to immediately change your trust in that user to 'none' or 'untrusted', and thereby affect the trust scores displayed for that user's comment on everyone else's page who has you in their web of trust.

I suspect something like this will emerge in the long run as a peer-to-peer solution once Web 2.0 begin loosing steam and we go through a few more of these boom and bust cycles.

Anything that's on the main internet can be killed by domain name, but it's all just a game of whack-a-mole.

Technically it's entirely possible to create a purely decentralized free speech forum that literally nobody owns. You can use similar technology to what powers bitcoin. And on the topic of domain name you could also even create a decentralized domain name system. There the implementation is a lot less clear on the best way to in determine distribution fairness, but there's plenty of interesting and viable options. The concept of a commoditizing an algorithmic proof of work from bitcoin is an obvious idea but a very nice and highly transferrable one. In English, a way of proving that an individual has had their computer do an average of 10 "minutes" of work. So perhaps domains could be openly "sold" for a day of work. I say "sold" because nobody actually receives any payment, but you lose a day of work and are allowed to claim a domain in return.

There's a mature (15 years in the making) peer-to-peer platform for censorship-resistant communication called FreeNet that (in theory) seems very strong against any monkey business. The key to its success is that every bit of the content on the network is distributed and hosted in an encrypted form between all users and a tor onion-routing like system where requests are bounced through multiple nodes.

That means, if you're using freenet you are also helping host the content as it was intended and helping others access content in a difficult-to-track manner. As others request freenet content some of the delivery will come from your local hosting cache. That being said, you can't look at what freenet content you host or manipulate it.

Also notable is the way you publish freenet content. Instead of making a server and setting up a service to allow others to make requests for information, you insert content (images, movies, html, etc) into the network. After that finishes you get a link that you can share.

Though like Tor or I2P, it's slow and demands a little technical care to get running. But that shouldn't be a problem for someone who really needs a robust method to get information out.

Last time I researched the system for a journalism class in Uni users had made chatrooms, forums, listservs, and a twitter clone. There are also a bunch of freenet blogs (flogs) filled with developer content and the usual conspiracy stuff.
